nameStory: Canada mint gets its name from being one of the most widespread native mints across Canada and northern North America. Unlike many of its European cousins that were brought over by settlers, this hardy mint has been growing wild in North American wetlands for thousands of years. It's our continent's own contribution to the wonderful world of minty plants!
description: Canada mint is a native North American wildflower that grows 1-2 feet tall in wet areas near ponds, streams, and marshes. This upright plant has the classic square stems that all mints share, along with opposite leaves that release that familiar minty scent when crushed. In summer, it produces small clusters of tiny bluish or pale violet flowers tucked where the upper leaves meet the stem, creating a subtle but lovely display.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Rub the opposite leaves between your fingers - they'll release a fresh, sweet minty fragrance that's unmistakably mint family. The leaves are oval with toothed edges and feel slightly fuzzy.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Feel the stem - it's distinctly square rather than round, a telltale sign of the mint family. The plant grows upright to about 1-2 feet tall with a somewhat bushy appearance.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Look for tiny bluish or pale violet flowers clustered in the leaf axils (where leaves meet the stem) rather than at the tip of the plant. Each flower is small but when many cluster together they create noticeable patches of color.

idTips.label: Habitat Clue
idTips.description: Found in consistently moist soil near water but not actually standing in water - think marsh edges, stream banks, or wet meadows where your feet might sink slightly into soggy ground.

habitat: Canada mint thrives in the wet, muddy edges of New England's marshes, ponds, streams, and lake shores. You'll find it in that sweet spot where the soil stays consistently moist but isn't underwater - often growing alongside cattails, sedges, and other water-loving plants. It particularly loves the rich, organic soils of wetland margins from sea level up into the mountains.

seasonality.spring: New growth emerges as the weather warms, with fresh green shoots appearing in wet areas. The distinctive square stems and opposite leaves make identification possible even without flowers.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from July through August, when the small bluish-violet flower clusters appear in the upper leaf joints. This is when the plant is most easily identified and the minty scent is strongest.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and the plant begins to die back, but crushed leaves still retain their minty fragrance. Seeds develop and disperse during this time.
seasonality.winter: The above-ground parts die back completely, leaving only underground rhizomes (root-like stems) that will send up new shoots next spring.

funFact: Canada mint is one of the primary sources of natural menthol used in medicines and candies worldwide - this humble wetland plant growing quietly along New England streams contains the same cooling compounds that make your breath mints tingle!
confusionNotes: Canada mint can be confused with other wild mints, but remember the flower location trick: Canada mint flowers cluster where the leaves meet the stem (in the leaf axils), while spearmint and other common mints have their flowers in spikes at the top of the plant. When in doubt, trust your nose - they'll all smell minty!
contextualKnowledge: Don't let the name fool you - Canada mint isn't just found in Canada! It's actually native throughout most of North America and was here long before European settlers arrived with their garden mints. The scientific name 'canadensis' simply means 'of Canada' because that's where European botanists first formally described it.
compareHints: Canada mint differs from its relatives by having flowers clustered in the leaf joints rather than in terminal spikes like spearmint, and it's strictly a wetland plant while corn mint tolerates drier soils. Unlike the strongly scented apple mint with its fuzzy white leaves, Canada mint has greener, less hairy foliage with a cleaner, less fruity mint scent.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Spearmint differs from other New England mints by its nearly hairless leaves and sweet, mild fragrance.
Unlike spearmint and peppermint which form terminal flower spikes, corn mint's flowers cluster in whorls around the stem at leaf joints.
Among New England's mints, apple mint stands out immediately for its fuzzy, rounded leaves that feel like velvet.
Unlike Canada mint which prefers moist but not waterlogged soils, watermint truly loves having wet feet and grows right at the water's edge.
Horse mint differs from our common native Canada mint by being much taller and having woolly-white stems rather than smooth ones.
